## Rethinking What Desire "Should" Look Like

Many of us grew up with a single story about desire: it strikes like lightning, it's spontaneous, and if you don't feel it instantly, something must be wrong. This cultural script — reinforced by movies, music, and even well-meaning advice — has left many people feeling broken when their experience of desire doesn't match the Hollywood version.

The truth is far more interesting and far more liberating.

## Dr. Rosemary Basson's Responsive Desire Model

In 2000, sex researcher Dr. Rosemary Basson challenged the dominant linear model of desire by introducing a circular model that better reflects how many people actually experience wanting. In Basson's model, desire doesn't always come first. Instead, the cycle often begins with **willingness** — being open to a sexual experience for any number of reasons: emotional closeness, curiosity, pleasure, or simply wanting to connect with a partner.

From that willingness, **arousal** begins. And from arousal, **desire** follows. This is called **responsive desire** — desire that emerges in response to arousing stimuli rather than appearing out of nowhere.

## Spontaneous vs. Responsive Desire

**Spontaneous desire** is what most people think of as "normal" — a seemingly random urge for sexual activity that appears without any specific trigger. Some people experience this frequently, and that's perfectly normal.

**Responsive desire** is equally normal. It means you may not think about sex until something activates your interest — a partner's touch, an emotional conversation, a romantic environment, or your own intentional engagement with erotic material. Many people find that once they're engaged in intimacy, their desire grows and deepens.

Research suggests that responsive desire is extremely common, particularly (but not exclusively) among women, people in long-term relationships, and people navigating stress or life transitions. Having responsive desire is not low desire — it's a different pathway to the same destination.

## The Full Spectrum of Desire

Desire exists on a wide spectrum. Some people experience strong spontaneous desire throughout their lives. Others experience primarily responsive desire. Many people move between the two depending on their life circumstances, relationships, stress levels, hormonal changes, and overall wellbeing.

Some people identify as asexual and experience little or no sexual desire — and this too is a completely valid experience. Desire is not a measure of your worth, your love, or your normalcy.

## A Trauma-Informed Perspective

Many people carry shame about their desire patterns because they were never taught that diversity in desire is normal. If you've ever felt "broken" because your desire doesn't look like what you see in media or hear from friends, that feeling makes sense — but it's based on incomplete information, not on anything wrong with you.

Learning about responsive desire is, for many people, a profoundly healing experience. It reframes their relationship with their own sexuality from one of inadequacy to one of understanding and self-compassion.

## Try It Tonight

**Takes about 3 minutes.**

Think of the last time you felt desire. Did it come out of nowhere, or after something had already started (a kiss, a good talk, time to relax)? Write one line about it. Both are normal.

## Your Sexual Response Has Two Systems

Imagine driving a car. You have an accelerator and a brake. Both are essential — the accelerator gets you moving, and the brake keeps you safe. Your sexual response system works the same way, according to the **Dual Control Model** developed by researchers Erick Janssen and John Bancroft at the Kinsey Institute.

## The Sexual Excitation System (Accelerators)

Your **Sexual Excitation System (SES)** is everything that activates your sexual interest and arousal. These are your accelerators — the things that make you think, "Yes, I want this."

Common accelerators include:
- Physical touch from a partner you're attracted to
- Feeling emotionally connected and safe
- Novelty and anticipation
- Erotic thoughts, fantasies, or material
- Feeling confident and attractive in your body
- A relaxing, private environment

Everyone's accelerators are calibrated differently. What turns one person on may do nothing for another — and that's perfectly normal.

## The Sexual Inhibition System (Brakes)

Your **Sexual Inhibition System (SIS)** is everything that reduces or suppresses your sexual response. These are your brakes — the things that make your body and mind say, "Not right now."

Common brakes include:
- Stress from work, finances, or family
- Body image concerns or self-consciousness
- Relationship conflict or unresolved tension
- Fear of unwanted outcomes (pregnancy, STIs, judgment)
- Depression, anxiety, or trauma responses
- Feeling rushed, pressured, or obligated
- Physical discomfort or pain
- Medications (antidepressants, hormonal contraceptives)

## Why "Just Relax" Doesn't Work

When someone is struggling with desire or arousal, the common advice is to "just relax" or "try harder." The dual control model explains why this advice fails: if your brakes are being pressed hard, pushing harder on the accelerator won't get you moving. You need to **release the brakes first**.

This means that addressing stress, creating safety, resolving relationship tension, and building a context that feels good are often more important than adding more stimulation.

## Sensitive Brakes Are Not Dysfunction

Some people have very sensitive brakes — meaning that even small amounts of stress, distraction, or self-consciousness can significantly reduce their desire. This is not a disorder. In fact, sensitive brakes serve a protective function: they help you avoid sexual situations that might be unsafe or unsatisfying.

Understanding your own brake/accelerator balance is one of the most empowering things you can do for your sexual wellbeing. Instead of asking "What's wrong with me?" you can ask, "What are my brakes, and what can I do to reduce them? What are my accelerators, and how can I activate them?"

## Context Is Everything

The dual control model highlights a crucial insight: sexual response is not just about what's happening to your body. It's about the **context** — your emotional state, your relationship dynamics, your environment, your stress level, and your sense of safety. Creating a context where brakes are minimized and accelerators are activated is the foundation of satisfying sexual experiences.

## Try It Tonight

**Takes about 5 minutes.**

Make two short lists: three things that turn you on (accelerators) and three things that shut desire down (brakes), such as stress, mess or feeling rushed. Pick one brake you can ease this week.

## Desire Discrepancy Is Normal

One of the most common concerns people bring to therapists and relationship discussions is desire discrepancy — when partners want sex at different frequencies or in different ways. Many people interpret this as a sign that their relationship is failing, that their partner doesn't love them, or that they themselves are inadequate.

The reality is that **desire discrepancy is one of the most normal experiences in human relationships**. No two people will ever want exactly the same thing at exactly the same time for the entirety of a relationship. This is not a problem to solve — it's a reality to navigate with compassion and communication.

## New Relationship Energy (NRE)

*Building on earlier lessons: you met NRE in Emotional Intelligence & Self-Regulation. Here the question is what it does to desire.*

**New Relationship Energy (NRE)** is the intense excitement, passion and sometimes obsessive thinking that comes with a new connection. Most people know it as the honeymoon phase. NRE can feel like a flood of spontaneous desire, making it easy to confuse the intensity of novelty with the depth of connection.

NRE fades for every couple, usually within a year or two, and that is normal. It does not mean the relationship is failing. For people with more than one partner, NRE with someone new can temporarily lower desire toward established partners. Love has not diminished. The brain's novelty-seeking systems are switched on. Understanding NRE through the lens of Basson's model helps: NRE provides intense external stimulation (accelerators), while established relationships may require more intentional context-creation.

## Navigating Desire Differences

When partners have different desire patterns, the key is to move from blame to curiosity:

**Instead of:** "You never want to have sex" or "You always want sex"
**Try:** "I notice our desire patterns are different right now. Can we talk about what each of us needs?"

Strategies that many people find helpful include:
- **Scheduling intimacy**: This isn't unromantic — it's intentional. Just as you schedule quality time, scheduling intimate connection honors its importance.
- **Expanding the definition of intimacy**: Not every intimate encounter needs to include sex. Massage, cuddling, bathing together, or simply being physically close can nurture connection.
- **Taking turns initiating**: If one partner always initiates, the other may feel pressured. Sharing initiation creates balance.
- **Checking in about brakes**: Often, the "lower desire" partner has more active brakes (stress, exhaustion, unresolved conflict) than weak accelerators.

## Basson's Model in Your Relationships

**If you're single or dating:** Early dating brings novelty, which sparks spontaneous desire. Do not judge your whole sex drive by it.

**If you have one partner:** In long relationships, responsive desire is the norm. Start with closeness and let desire follow.

**If you have more than one partner:** In ENM contexts, Basson's responsive desire model offers valuable insight: different partners may activate different desire patterns in you. You might experience spontaneous desire with one partner and responsive desire with another — and both are equally valid expressions of your sexuality.

This understanding can reduce comparison and self-judgment. Instead of wondering "Why do I want them more than I want my other partner?" you can recognize that desire is contextual, relational, and always changing.

## Communication Without Pressure

The most important skill for navigating desire in relationships is learning to talk about it without creating pressure. Pressure is one of the most powerful brakes in the dual control model. When someone feels that they "should" want sex or that their partner will be disappointed, their brakes engage even harder.

Creating a culture in your relationships where desire can be discussed openly — without obligation, disappointment, or shame — is one of the greatest gifts you can offer your partners and yourself.

## Try It Tonight

**Takes about 3 minutes.**

Finish this sentence: "I feel most open to closeness when ___." Share it with a partner without asking for anything, or save it for someone you date later.

## Desire Is a Garden, Not a Light Switch

One of the most liberating shifts in understanding desire is moving from thinking of it as something that either happens or doesn't — like a light switch — to understanding it as something you can cultivate, like a garden. Gardens need attention, the right conditions, and patience. Desire works the same way.

## Mindfulness and Embodiment

Many people are disconnected from their bodies — they live in their heads, managing responsibilities, worrying about the future, or replaying the past. This disconnection makes it difficult to notice the subtle cues of desire and arousal.

**Embodiment practices** help you reconnect with your physical experience:
- **Body scanning**: Take a few minutes to notice sensations throughout your body without judgment. Where do you feel tension? Pleasure? Warmth? Numbness?
- **Mindful touch**: Whether touching yourself or being touched by a partner, practice bringing your full attention to the sensation rather than thinking about what comes next.
- **Breathwork**: Slow, deep breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system (rest and digest), which supports sexual arousal. Quick, shallow breathing activates the sympathetic nervous system (fight or flight), which suppresses it.

These practices are valuable for everyone, and many people find them especially healing if they have a history of disconnection from their bodies due to trauma, shame, or simply living in a culture that doesn't encourage embodied awareness.

## The Role of Context

Dr. Emily Nagoski, building on the dual control model, emphasizes that **context is the key variable** in desire. The same touch, the same partner, the same activity can feel completely different depending on the context.

Creating desire-supportive contexts might include:
- Reducing environmental stressors before intimate time
- Building anticipation through flirtatious communication
- Creating physical spaces that feel comfortable, private, and inviting
- Addressing relationship conflicts before expecting sexual connection
- Making time for transition from "doing mode" to "being mode"

## Scheduling Intimacy

Many people resist the idea of scheduling intimacy because it feels "unromantic." But consider: you schedule everything else that matters to you — meals with friends, exercise, creative projects. Scheduling intimate time is simply prioritizing connection.

Scheduled intimacy doesn't have to mean scheduled sex. It can mean creating space where intimacy is possible — a date night, a morning with no plans, an evening with phones put away. What happens in that space can be whatever both partners want it to be.

## When to Seek Professional Support

Sometimes, changes in desire reflect something that would benefit from professional attention. Consider reaching out to a sex-positive therapist or AASECT-certified sex therapist if:
- Your desire has changed significantly and the change bothers you
- You and your partner(s) have been unable to navigate desire differences on your own
- You suspect that medications, hormonal changes, or health conditions may be contributing
- Past trauma is affecting your current sexual experience
- You feel distressed or disconnected from your sexuality

Seeking professional support is not a sign of failure — it's an act of self-care and investment in your wellbeing. A sex-positive therapist can help you understand your unique desire patterns and develop strategies that work for your life, your body, and your relationships.

## Desire Is Connection

At its core, desire is about connection — to yourself, to your body, to your partners, and to pleasure. Whether your desire is spontaneous, responsive, or somewhere in between, it is valid, it is normal, and it is yours to explore on your own terms.

## Try It Tonight

**Takes about 5 minutes.**

Spend five minutes on something that feels good to your senses and is not sexual: a hot shower, music, stretching. Keep your attention on the feeling. That is practice for desire.
